newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan oil firms urged to be as efficient as rivals.
newsitem.headline: Japan oil firms urged to be as efficient as rivals.

text.p: Japan's oil industry must try to bring its efficiency up to the level of its global rivals before a widely anticipated industry realignment can take place, the head of the Japanese unit of U.S. oil giant Exxon Corp said.
"In Japan there are 11 major players and that is probably more than there will be," William Innes, president of Esso Sekiyu K.K., said in an interview.
"However, we are in a sense, a long way from that position."
In comparison to the U.S. or European oil industry, Japanese oil firms have much room for improving efficiency before resorting to mergers, Innes said.
"Although, ultimately there will be coming a concentration within the Japanese industry, there are a number of necessary steps which will occur that are not necessarily mergers."
With profits at Japanese oil firms plunging and efforts to cut costs leading to increased cooperation, analysts expect a major industry reshuffle to occur sooner or later.

U.S. and European oil giants this year have announced plans to merge downstream operations because of thin margins. Texaco Inc and Shell Oil Co said earlier this month that they were discussing a downstream oil merger in the United States.
In late February, U.S. Mobil Corp's and British Petroleum Co said they planned to merge their European refineries and service stations.
The merger mania is not expected to affect Japan, as Texaco and BP are not present in Japan's retailing market, Innes said.

In Asian countries other than Japan, similar moves by the oil majors could occur, Innes said. However, characteristics of the Far East market, which is growing rapidly, differ greatly from the situation in Europe and the United States, he added.
In Japan, oil companies are facing sinking profits, largely due to reasons stemming from the liberalisation of oil product imports this April.
Before deregulation, imports of oil products such as gasoline, kerosene and gas oil were restricted to refiners. Now, in theory, any company can import petroleum products.

Innes said the deregulation has exposed the inefficiency of Japan's oil industry. The two largest inefficiencies are at the primary distribution and retailing stages, where further efforts to rationalise operations are needed immediately, he said.
As part of efforts to cut costs, many Japanese oil firms, including Esso Sekiyu, have agreed to cooperate in distribution with other oil firms.
Another major issue needed to be resolved is domestic oil product prices, Innes said.
In order to combat oil product imports, most Japanese refiners introduced in April a new wholesale pricing system which brings wholesale prices to international levels.
In effect, the wholesale price of gasoline was lowered while prices of kerosene and gas oil were raised.
Retail prices, however, have not managed to follow the changes in wholesale prices because of competition at gasoline stands and opposition from consumers.

"Gasoline prices are at about international levels but kerosene and gas oil are below the international market," Innes said. "We need to convince buyers in Japan that prices (of kerosene and gas oil) are too low," he said.

Innes said he could not completely agree with the wholesale pricing system. "I support 100 percent the broad concepts that Japanese prices should be basically in sync with international prices," Innes said.
However, it was not clear why prices throughout Japan have to be at similar levels, as various costs differ depending on the region, he said.
